1.label: 1(i)
1.explanation: Capillarity draws kerosene along narrow spaces in the wick.

1.label: 1(iii)
1.explanation: The original extension 0.005 m increases fourfold with four times the force.

1.label: 1(iv)
1.explanation: A pendulum exchanges gravitational potential and kinetic energy.

1.label: 1(v)
1.answer: The options do not supply an unambiguously correct example of mathematical language.
1.explanation: A numerical law such as density = mass/volume would be suitable. Option B incorrectly uses area, and the other choices are verbal descriptions.

1.label: 1(viii)
1.explanation: Elasticity is the ability to recover shape after unloading.

1.label: 1(ix)
1.explanation: The universe includes space, time, matter and energy.

2.explanation: Cohesion joins like molecules, adhesion joins unlike ones, viscosity opposes fluid-layer motion, surface tension acts along a liquid surface and capillarity changes liquid height in narrow tubes.

3.label: 3(a)
3.answer: Surface tension supports the carefully placed light needle; the ball breaks through and has insufficient buoyancy to float.
3.explanation: The needle must avoid breaking the surface. Its density alone does not explain this temporary support.

3.label: 3(b)
3.answer: Surface tension tends to minimise surface area, making small drops approximately spherical.
3.explanation: A sphere encloses a fixed volume with the least surface area; large falling drops can be distorted by air resistance.

4.label: 4(a)
4.answer: On Earth weight is approximately 10m newtons for mass m kilograms; on the Moon it is about one-sixth as much.
4.explanation: Mass stays the same while gravitational field strength changes.

4.label: 4(b)
4.explanation: The rocket’s mass is 10000/10=1000 kg; g on X=300/1000.

5.label: 5(a)(i)
5.answer: Mass measures inertia or matter quantity; weight is gravitational force.

5.label: 5(a)(ii)
5.answer: Mass has SI unit kilogram; weight has SI unit newton.
5.explanation: A force combines kg, m and s in kg·m/s².

5.label: 5(a)(iii)
5.answer: Mass is unchanged by moving between planets; weight changes with local gravity.
5.explanation: The same m is multiplied by different g.

5.label: 5(b)
5.explanation: Density=41.6/5.1≈8.16 g/cm³. Divide by water’s 1 g/cm³.

6.label: 6(a)(i)
6.answer: A ship encloses a large volume of air, lowering its average density.
6.explanation: The complete ship can be less dense than water despite its metal walls.

6.label: 6(a)(ii)
6.answer: The hull displaces enough water to provide an upward force equal to its weight.

6.label: 6(a)(iii)
6.answer: A compact coin displaces too little water before submerging.
6.explanation: Its weight exceeds the maximum buoyancy available for its small volume.

6.label: 6(b)
6.explanation: The upthrust is the displaced water’s weight, 1.1 N. Add it to the apparent weight 3.3 N.

7.label: 7(a)
7.answer: Pressure is force per unit area, rather than a force by itself.
7.explanation: Pressure has unit N/m² whereas force has unit N.

7.label: 7(b)
7.answer: For the same force, a sharper, smaller contact area produces greater pressure.
7.explanation: Cutting also depends on sharpness, blade shape and material; a knife can cut effectively when equally sharp.

8.label: 8(a)
8.answer: Dry low-pressure air can dry and irritate nasal tissues and contribute to bleeding; rapid pressure changes can also affect delicate vessels.
8.explanation: Altitude does not necessarily cause bleeding in everyone; a simple claim that blood pressure alone bursts all vessels is incomplete.

8.label: 8(b)
8.answer: The outside pressure decreases before pressure in the middle ear equalises. Yawning opens the Eustachian tube.
8.explanation: Air moves between the throat and middle ear to reduce the pressure difference across the eardrum.

9.label: 9(a)(i)
9.answer: Distance is total path length; displacement is directed change between endpoints.
9.explanation: Draw a curved path from A to B and a straight arrow A→B; label the curve distance and the arrow displacement.

9.label: 9(a)(ii)
9.answer: A round trip has positive distance and zero displacement.
9.explanation: Start and finish coincide, so there is no net position change.

9.label: 9(b)(i)
9.answer: 0 m/s at the end of the whole motion; 42 m/s at the end of the first stage.
9.explanation: The wording says it eventually stops. During acceleration v=10+4×8=42.

9.label: 9(b)(ii)
9.answer: Draw straight segments from (0,10) to (8,42), then to (16,0). Distance in the first 8 s is 208 m.
9.explanation: The velocity–time trapezium area is ½(10+42)×8.

10.label: 10(a)(i)
10.answer: Work is energy transferred by a force acting through displacement; unit joule.
10.explanation: W=Fs for force parallel to movement.

10.label: 10(a)(ii)
10.answer: Power is the rate of doing work; unit watt.

10.label: 10(a)(iii)
10.answer: Energy is the capacity to do work; unit joule.
10.explanation: It can change form while total energy is conserved.

10.label: 10(b)(i)
10.explanation: The cow’s pulling force has a component along the displacement.

10.label: 10(b)(ii)
10.answer: No mechanical work on a stationary book.
10.explanation: Its displacement is zero despite the upward support force.

10.label: 10(b)(iii)
10.answer: Yes, the aircraft gains gravitational potential energy.
10.explanation: The upward displacement requires work against gravity.

10.label: 10(b)(iv)
10.answer: Gravity does no work in level flight; engine thrust may do work against drag.
10.explanation: Weight is perpendicular to horizontal displacement. The net work is zero at constant speed.
